speaker: a
text: Axis one, compute topology. Where does rio run, what binds its lifetime, what's the cold start. On desktop, it's a native Rust binary — `frontends/rioterm` is the actual executable crate, depends on everything else. Lifetime is the OS window. One rio process per window, by default, though there's a config switch for multi-window-per-process. When you launch rio, the startup path is: `rio-window` creates a platform window — on Mac that's an NSWindow via objc bindings, on Linux it's Wayland or X11, on Windows it's a Win32 HWND — then `sugarloaf` initializes a `wgpu::Instance`, requests an adapter, creates a `wgpu::Device` and `wgpu::Queue`, allocates a swap chain surface tied to that window handle. That's the cold start. On a warm machine it's single-digit milliseconds past the binary load. The [JP: 描画] device is per-window. You can't share GPU state across rio windows without IPC.

speaker: b
text: So every window pays for its own GPU context?

speaker: a
text: Yes, but the adapter is shared at the driver level — wgpu is smart enough to let multiple devices coexist on one physical adapter. The real cost per window is the swap chain and the staging buffers for glyph atlases. Not huge. Call it ten, fifteen megabytes of VRAM per window baseline. Now the WASM target — this is where it gets interesting. When `sugarloaf` compiles with the `wasm-bindgen` feature, the same `wgpu` code paths hit WebGPU through the browser. Look at the root `Cargo.toml`: `wasm-bindgen = "0.2.87"`, `wasm-bindgen-futures`, `console_error_panic_hook` — those deps only exist because the renderer needs to bootstrap inside a browser tab. Lifetime there is the tab. Cold start is worse — you pay WASM instantiation plus WebGPU adapter negotiation, which can be two hundred to five hundred milliseconds depending on browser and driver.

speaker: a

text: Okay. And axis two, the LLM thing — this is a terminal, there's no model.

text: N/A here, rio isn't in that plane. Move on. Axis three, tool mechanics — what primitives does rio actually have its hands on. And here "tool" means the OS, not an agent's tool call. The primitive is the pseudoterminal. On Unix that's `openpty` — kernel allocates a master-slave pair, the master is a file descriptor rio holds, the slave is `dup2`'d onto the child shell's stdin, stdout, stderr. The `teletypewriter` crate is rio's abstraction over this. On Windows you can't openpty the same way because the NT kernel doesn't have pty semantics, so Microsoft ships ConPTY — the conhost subsystem — and `teletypewriter` has a Windows branch that talks to ConPTY via `CreatePseudoConsole`. Same API shape from rio's side, very different kernel underneath.

speaker: b
text: So rio launches bash or zsh or pwsh as a child process, and then just reads bytes off a file descriptor.

speaker: a
text: That's the physical layer. Then it has to parse those bytes. Shell output isn't plain text — it's plain text interleaved with escape sequences. `\x1b[31m` for red foreground, `\x1b[2J` for clear screen, `\x1b]0;title\x07` for OSC title set, DEC private modes, mouse tracking, bracketed paste, Sixel graphics, Kitty keyboard protocol, the whole VT100-plus-extensions stew. Parsing that is what the `copa` crate does. Copa is rio's fork of Alacritty's `vte` parser — it's a state machine that consumes bytes and emits parsed events: `Print('a')`, `CSI([31m)`, `OSC(0, "title")`. The frontend wires those events to a grid data structure. The grid lives in `rio-backend`. It's a two-dimensional array of `Cell` structs — each cell has a glyph, foreground color, background color, style bits. Scrollback is a ring buffer of rows above the visible viewport.

speaker: b
text: How big is that ring buffer?

speaker: a
text: Configurable. Default is around ten thousand rows. We'll come back to this on the context axis because it matters. Axis four, extension loading. Rio is config-driven, not plugin-driven. There's no dylib loader, no Lua runtime like wezterm, no kitty-style remote control protocol — though some of that is on the roadmap. What you get is a TOML config at `~/.config/rio/config.toml` on Linux, equivalent paths elsewhere. The config has sections for colors, fonts, keybindings, window behavior, shell, navigation. Themes are TOML files referenced by name; rio ships a handful and you can drop your own in a `themes/` directory. Fonts are resolved through the system font provider plus `sugarloaf/src/font/` which handles shaping — rio uses `swash` for font introspection and shaping, visible as `font_introspector` inside `sugarloaf/src`. Hot reload exists for config — there's a file watcher via `rio-notifier`, which wraps `notify` under the hood. Change a color in the TOML, rio picks it up within a tick. That's the extension story. Lean. Opinionated. No [JP: 画像 (がぞう) — image]-plugin system.

speaker: b

You cannot ship your own yet. Axis five, context strategy — and this is where I want to slow down because it maps surprisingly well onto LLM context reasoning. Terminal scrollback is the analog. You have a finite buffer. You have arriving data. You have to decide what to keep verbatim, what to compress, what to evict, and how to recall it when the user searches.

speaker: b

speaker: a
text: Rio's grid in `rio-backend` keeps the visible viewport in a dense 2D array — rows times columns, one Cell per character. Above the viewport, scrollback is a VecDeque of rows. When the deque hits the configured max, the oldest row is dropped. That's the eviction policy — pure FIFO, no heuristics. There's no "important" row detection. No summarization. If you run a long compile and it emits fifty thousand lines and your scrollback limit is ten thousand, forty thousand lines are gone. Compare that to how an LLM agent manages context — usually there's a compaction step, keep the first system prompt, keep recent turns verbatim, summarize middle turns. Rio doesn't do that. It's pure recency. But — and this is the clever part — rio keeps style metadata per cell, which means a copy-on-search through scrollback stays color-aware, and the search implementation in `rio-backend` uses regex — the `regex = "1.12.3"` in the workspace Cargo is exactly for this.

The [JP: 記録 (きろく) — record] of your session is in memory only by default; rio doesn't persist scrollback across restarts, though you can pipe through `tmux` or `screen` if you want durability.

text: 日本 語 で 一 行 に まとめる と — summarized in one line in Japanese — デスクトップ だけ で 良い なら Alacritty で 十分、ブラウザ で 端末 を 描画 したい なら rio — if desktop alone is enough, Alacritty suffices; if you want to render terminals in the browser, rio. もう 一 つ の 言い方 — another way to say it — 画面 の 描画 を 場所 に 依存 させない ために、rio は クレート を 分けた — in order to make screen rendering not depend on the location, rio split its crates. 画像 と 光 と 動き を どこ で も 同じ 流れ で 表示する ために、sugarloaf が 独立 して いる — in order to display image and light and motion with the same flow everywhere, sugarloaf stands independent. これ が 今日 の 核心 — this is today's core. 他 の 端末 は 描画 を ネイティブ に 縛った、rio は 縛らなかった、それ だけ の 話 — other terminals bound rendering to native, rio did not, that's the whole story.
